content: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN) is a condition that arises due to delayed clearance of lung fluid, leading to rapid breathing in newborns. It is a frequent reason for full-term infants to be admitted to neonatal intensive care units, particularly following elective caesarean sections. Standard treatment typically involves administering oxygen and, in some cases, using continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). Most affected infants also receive antibiotics. Accelerating the removal of lung fluid could potentially reduce the duration of symptoms and minimize complications. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether the use of diuretics could decrease the duration of oxygen therapy, alleviate respiratory symptoms, and shorten hospital stays in term infants diagnosed with TTN. To address this, an updated search was conducted in September 2015 across several databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, PubMed, and CINAHL. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared diuretic administration to placebo or no treatment in infants less than seven days old, born at 37 weeks of gestation or later, and presenting with clinical signs of TTN. Data collection and analysis followed the guidelines outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Two reviewers independently assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. The previous systematic review included two trials involving a total of 100 infants with TTN. The updated search did not identify any new trials. The first trial (Wiswell 1985) randomized 50 infants to receive either oral furosemide (2 mg/kg at diagnosis, followed by 1 mg/kg 12 hours later if tachypnoea persisted) or a placebo. The second trial (Karabayir 2006) randomized 50 infants to receive either intravenous furosemide (2 mg/kg) or an equivalent volume of normal saline placebo. Neither trial reported on the need for respiratory support. Furthermore, neither study demonstrated a statistically significant effect of furosemide on the duration of symptoms or the length of hospital stay in infants with TTN. Based on the available evidence, diuretics cannot be recommended as a treatment for TTN. Their use should be avoided unless further data become available. This conclusion suggests that furosemide may not effectively promote the resorption of lung fluid, or that other factors beyond delayed fluid clearance contribute to the development of TTN. It remains uncertain whether administering furosemide to the infant—or even to the mother prior to a caesarean section—might reduce the duration of the illness. Given the continued high rates of elective caesarean sections, these interventions could warrant further investigation in future trials.
